source.title: The Information of Large Language Model Geometry
source.authors: Zhiquan Tan; Chenghai Li; Weiran Huang

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws and offers a theoretical account, but it does not test the specified loss-scaling, extrapolation, allocation, architecture, modality, or downstream-predictability claims. Its simulation concerns representation entropy, not held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports a simulated relationship between normalized representation entropy and model size, using matrix-entropy data from cited work [25]. This is related to scaling but is not a measurement of held-out cross-entropy loss, so it does not test any listed version. The paper’s statements about empirical loss scaling cite prior work; they are not results from this study. The information-gain, regression, and sentence-distance results concern different measures.
record.test_reason: The paper offers a theoretical (conditional-entropy, skill-graph) derivation of scaling laws and a simulated plot of normalized representation entropy versus model size built from data in cited work [25]. It reports no held-out pretraining loss, extrapolation, allocation, architecture, modality or downstream measurement, so no version is tested. Representation entropy is a related but different construct from loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors simulate representation entropy and report a power law with model size, then derive scaling laws in N, compute and D from a conditional-entropy, skill-learning theory under stated assumptions. The rest of the paper covers information gain and ridge regression, Lasso versus attention, and token-distributed information. None of it is an empirical test of loss scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops a theoretical account of scaling using skills and conditional entropy, and simulates representation entropy from data in [25]; it does not reproduce the original loss-scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The simulated normalized representation entropy (rate-distortion estimate, epsilon 0.1, from matrix-entropy data in [25]) follows a power law with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized representation entropy of LLM embeddings follows a power law in model size.

record.problems: The representation-entropy result is a simulation based on data from cited work, rather than a direct measurement of held-out loss. The theoretical account relies on stated assumptions, including sequential learning of skills and invariant distribution differences; the paper does not empirically test the listed claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the claim versions. Figures 3–6 and the regression examples report information-gain or sentence-geometry findings, not outcomes measuring the listed scaling claims.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. The paper only derives it theoretically and cites Kaplan et al.
Extrapolation from small to large runs.
Effect of depth, width or other shape details at fixed parameter count.
Downstream task performance versus scale or loss. The prompting theorems are theoretical only.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on setup and fitting choices, and curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical exponents (O(N^-alpha), O(S^-alpha/(alpha+2)), O(D^(1-2gamma))) are derivations, not measurements. A researcher could treat them as a theoretical account bearing on V1, but there are no results to label. The Pythia information-gain results (Figure 3) vary with model size but measure a different construct and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; the specified multi-order-of-magnitude behavior.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-budget sweeps and the growth of loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Measured downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Empirical dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and evidence of curves bending away from a power law.
